B2|eIho2S0ZahI|2.author: Julian Treasure
B2|eIho2S0ZahI|2.passage: Listening is a skill, and like every skill it gets stronger with practice.  If you want to listen better, the simplest move is to be present instead of planning your reply while someone is still talking.  When a client speaks, your first job is to understand, not to defend.  One useful technique is to listen for the feeling behind the words.  If someone says it feels busy, they might really be saying they feel confused or overwhelmed.  You can't respond to that until you hear it.  Then, before you answer, paraphrase what you heard.  You can say, what I'm hearing is that you want it to feel simpler.  Is that right?  That one line makes the other person feel respected, and it catches misunderstandings early.  When people feel truly heard, they relax.  Once they relax, they can actually take in your answer.

B2|eIho2S0ZahI|3.passage: Before you answer, take one breath in through your nose, let it out slowly, and then speak.  That brief pause gives the other person space and makes you sound considered.  You can also lower your pitch slightly at the ends of important sentences.  A voice that keeps rising can sound like it's asking for permission. C2|BSxg87CoOu4|2.title: Ending a conversation well
C2|BSxg87CoOu4|2.author: The Futur
C2|BSxg87CoOu4|2.passage: A meeting without a clear ending is a meeting that repeats itself.  Before I say goodbye, I spend one minute summarizing what we decided.  I'll say, so today we chose this direction, you'll send the final text by Thursday, and I'll deliver the revised version the following Tuesday.  Then I ask, does that match your understanding?  That question catches confusion while everyone is still in the room.  If something is wrong, we fix it now instead of through a long email thread.  Next, I state the single next action and who owns it.  People leave a clear meeting feeling confident, even if the work isn't finished.  They know what happens next.  Finally I thank the client for their feedback, because good feedback is valuable.  A warm, organized close makes you look professional and makes the client feel safe.  It's a small habit, but it's one of the strongest signals that you know what you're doing.
